Posted July 6, 2001
Analysis by Richard Cowan

Cannabis has been a schedule 1 drug in the UK since 1971, when the World Health Organization pronounced it medically useless.

Last year The British Medical Journal made a mediocre contribution to the cannabis debate.
See
British Medical Journal Says It Wants To Improve " The Quality of the Cannabis " But Offers Too Little Too Late
Now they are at it again, with two articles and an editorial and the same pretense of objectivity.
See
Cannabinoids for pain and nausea

These articles have resulted in the usual wretched media coverage, some of which came from sources that should know better.

First, it should be understood that no new research was done for these articles. This was a review of the medical literature on studies dating back to the 1970s.

Second, none of the studies involved the use of whole cannabis, just isolated synthetic cannabinoids.

Consequently, the basic error in the BMJ articles, reflected in the media coverage, was to assume that the same results would apply to whole cannabis and focus on the use of isolated cannabinoids, usually just THC, and then assume that this was the same – or better – than whole cannabis.

As the pain article said, " No randomised controlled trialsevaluated cannabis; all tested active substances were cannabinoids. Oral delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) 5-20 mg, an oral syntheticnitrogen analogue of THC 1 mg, and intramuscular levonantradol1.5-3 mg were about as effective as codeine 50-120 mg, and oralbenzopyranoperidine 2-4 mg was less effective than codeine 60-120mg and no better than placebo. Adverse effects, most often psychotropic,werecommon.
Conclusion: Cannabinoids are no more effective than codeinein controlling pain and have depressant effects on the centralnervous system that limit their use. Their widespread introductioninto clinical practice for pain management is therefore undesirable.In acute postoperative pain they should not be used. Before cannabinoidscan be considered for treating spasticity and neuropathic pain,further valid randomised controlled studies areneeded. "

First, there are around 60 cannabinoids, so testing a few isolated cannabinoids and then claiming that this would apply to all cannabinoids is unjustified. It is even less justifiable to assume that this would apply to whole cannabis with the full range of cannabinoids, which may well work synergistically.

In fact, this point is the very essence of the medical marijuana debate in countries in which THC is legally available.
See
Marinol Was The First Schedule 2 Drug To Be " Down-Scheduled, "
Boasts Roxanne On Its New Marinol.com Web Site.
Doesn’t That Mean That It Should Never Have Been Schedule 2 Anyway?
and links

The BMJ Editorial " Cannabinoids for pain and nausea " by Eija Kalso, associate professor. Pain Clinic, Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine, Helsinki University Hospital, ends with this comment:

" Future research may provide us with better cannabinoid compounds with potential new therapeutic applications.10 However,the current information is that the adverse effects of cannabinoidsoutweigh their effectiveness. 1112 About a year ago in theBMJ Strang et al asked for a more informed debate about the therapueticuse of cannabinoids,13 and this week's two systematic reviewscontribute to this debate. On current evidence cannabinoids canbe recommended only for use in controlled clinical trials in carefullyselected conditions for which there is no effective treatment.The launch of the first large multicentre trial on cannabis inthe control of pain and tremors in multiple sclerosis14 is thefirst step on thisway. "

Notice the footnotes.
10. Piomelli D, Giuffrida A, Calignano A, de Fonseca FR. The endocannabinoid system as a target for therapeutic drugs. Trends Pharmacol Sci 2000; 21: 218-224[Medline].

11. Institute of Medicine. Marijuana and medicine. Washington, DC: National Academy Press, 1999.

12. Hall W, Solowij N. Adverse effects of cannabis. Lancet 1998; 352: 1611-1616[Medline].

13. Strang J, Witton J, Hall W. Improving the quality of the cannabis debate: defining the different domains. BMJ 2000; 320: 108-110[Full Text].

14. Dyer O. Cannabis trial launched in patients with MS. BMJ 2001; 322: 192[Full Text]

The statement that " the current information is that the adverse effects of cannabinoidsoutweigh their effectiveness " is supported by notes 11 and 12.

However, note 11 is the IOM report that recommended that whole smoked cannabis be made immediately available, and based its objections to its extended use on the supposed problems with smoking, ignoring vaporization.
See
Executive Summary Of The IOM Report, Marijuana And Medicine: Assessing The Science Base

Note 12 was an article in the Lancet by Wayne Hall, which had other problems.
See
Australian Study of Medical Cannabis Recommends Limited Exemptions for Patients. Misrepresents House Of Lords Report and MAPS/NORML Vaporization Studies.
and links

But even Hall accepts smoking marijuana on an interim basis -- until " Future research may provide us with better cannabinoid compounds with potential new therapeutic applications " as Kalso puts it.

All of this makes it even odder that the BMJ studies ignored whole cannabis, especially considering that there are now tests under way in the UK by GW Pharmaceuticals, using a solution derived from whole cannabis. But there are other problems as well. The negative conclusions do not always follow from the statements in the articles.

Consider the following statement from the article on anti-emetics:
" Overwhelmingly, patients preferred cannabinoids for future chemotherapy,even though cannabinoids were only slightly more effective thanother antiemetics and only for moderately emetogenic chemotherapy.Patients' subjective view on preference is more important thanthe scientifically evaluated efficacy of that intervention. Althoughside effects occur more often with cannabinoids, these may beconcentrated in a fairly small number of patients so that mostpatients find cannabinoids effective without undue adverse effects.There are even some potentially beneficial side effects. Of 100cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy who received a cannabinoid 30 more would be sedated, 20 would feel a sensation of a " high, " and 15 would feel euphoric compared with 100 who received a conventionalantiemetic. Some patients may perceive a degree of sedation orsomnolence as useful during chemotherapy. Thus, further clinicaltrials with cannabinoids in chemotherapy arejustified. " (Emphasis added)

And the article on pain seems to be largely a straw man argument. No one is claiming that cannabis – by itself - was likely to be effective in dealing acute pain, much less that these synthetic cannabinoids are.

However, many patients find whole cannabis helpful in dealing with long-term – chronic – pain, because it does not have the debilitating effects of most pharmaceutical pain relievers.

Moreover, many patients seem to use cannabis in conjunction with other – more powerful pain relievers – to reduce the dose required. And the pain article even notes such use: " Level of morphineuse for breakthrough pain was significantly lower, however, whilethe patient was taking THC than while taking placebo (170 mg v410 mg per three weeks). In a patient with neuropathic pain andspasticity secondary to a spinal cord ependymoma, THC 5 mg andcodeine 50 mg were equianalgesic, and both were superior to placebo. Only THC, however, had a beneficial effect onspasticity. " (Emphasis added)

The article does recognize that there are not adequate treatments for neuropathic pain – pain originating in the nerves, not the direct result of a problem elsewhere – but it says " Before cannabinoidscan be considered for treating spasticity and neuropathic pain,further valid randomised controlled studies areneeded. " Fine, but this would not follow from the data in the article.

Oddly, in one of the few references to smoked marijuana, it says, " We found no trialsevaluating smoked cannabis for pain management, but one trialcompared the effect of smoked marijuana with smoked placebo onpostural balance in patients with spastic multiple sclerosis.16The smoked marijuana was associated with subjective improvementof symptoms and with objectively measured impaired posture andbalance in allsubjects. "

16. Greenberg HS, Werness SA, Pugh JE, Andrus RO, Anderson DJ, Domino EF. Short-term effects of smoking marijuana on balance in patients with multiple sclerosis and normal volunteers. Clin Pharmacol Ther 1994; 55: 324-328[Medline].

I say that this was " odd " because that is one of the few studies that claim to show that marijuana worsened the MS symptoms. It says, " Smoking one marijuana cigarette containing 1.54% delta 9-tetrahydrocannabinol increased postural tracking error in both the patients and normal control subjects with both eyes open and closed; this untoward effect was greatest for the patients. The tracking error was also accompanied by a decrease in response speed for the patients with their eyes closed. Marijuana smoking further impairs posture and balance in patients with spastic MS "

That is the exact opposite of what the BJM article says! This does not give me a lot of confidence in their review.

Now, there are thousands of MS patients in the UK and DEAland illegally using medical marijuana for symptomatic relief and the GW Pharmaceutical trials are reporting very positive results, so this study was definitely an exception. Maybe the 1.54% marijuana was just too weak!

Nonetheless, combined with their dubious citations as noted about the other footnotes – above – I find myself with serious doubts about this work on its own terms.

In any case, what we have here is a review of the literature on studies of cannabinoids, not marijuana. No one thinks that enough is known about isolated cannabinoids to say that they have an established place in medicine beyond the limited use of Marinol, which depends on marijuana prohibition for most of its market. On the other hand, there is an enormous interest in medical marijuana right now.

So this is really a sort of bait-and-switch. It is really just prohibitionist propaganda.

In fact, it has already been used by one of the candidates for the UK Conservative Party leadership, Kenneth Clark to justify his opposition to legalizing non-medical cannabis in the UK.

He is quoted today as saying, " There is a study out of Nottingham University which says it does have a depressant effect if taken in large doses and even queries whether it has any medical benefit. "

Of course, this utterly contemptible twit is also the Deputy Director of British American Tobacco.

Really. We couldn’t make this up.

But the point is that these articles have already been used to justify arresting people, and we will hear more about them from the prohibitionists, who will never have read them.

That appears to be the case at the New York Times, whose web site had the Reuters article below.. The worst of the bunch.

July 6, 2001
From The New York Times

SCIENTISTS STUB OUT CANNABIS AS WONDERDRUG
(MarijuanaNews note: Notice the marijuana related pun in the headline. Also notice the use of the word " scientists " indicating that this is a definitive work backed by a " scientific consensus. " )

LONDON ( Reuters ) - Cannabis is no better than codeine at controlling pain and a series of undesirable side effects means it has no place at present in mainstream medicine, scientists said on Friday.

After trawling through 39 past clinical studies on its use in easing pain and nausea, two groups of researchers writing in the British Medical Journal poured cold water on the idea that cannabis was a neglected wonderdrug.
(MarijuanaNews note: Cannabis is one thing only when it is whole cannabis, marijuana.)

" It hasn't turned out to be a great success. There are, at the moment, much better alternatives, " Eija Kalso, associate professor in the Department of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine at Helsinki University Hospital, told Reuters.

Future research might provide better cannabinoids -- the active substances in cannabis -- which could help treat multiple sclerosis ( MS ) and nerve damage pain, but current information suggested adverse effects outweighed the benefits, she said.

" On current evidence cannabinoids can be recommended only for use in controlled clinical trials in carefully selected conditions for which there is no effective treatment, " Kalso concluded in an editorial in the magazine.

Interest in the therapeutic use of cannabis has grown recently, and patient groups in a number of countries have called for freer availability. Thousands of MS sufferers are already breaking the law by buying the drug from street dealers.
(MarijuanaNews note: Notice the switch to medical marijuana – whole cannabis! And would they buy something that is making their symptoms worse?)

GW Pharmaceuticals Plc, a recently listed British company which aims to develop the world's first cannabis-based medicines, is currently conducting trials to try to prove the value of cannabis extracts in treating MS and cancer pain.

Side Effects

Fiona Campbell of the Pain Management Centre at Queen's Medical Centre in Nottingham, England -- who led the study on pain -- said cannabinoids compared poorly with modern medicines in controlling acute pain.

Furthermore, there were many adverse effects -- including cognitive impairment, psychosis, blurred vision and palpitations -- which limited its use.

Campbell said carefully selected cannabis derivatives might yet help some MS patients or those with complex pain, but more research was needed before it was put into clinical use.

" You can't have the process in reverse -- you cannot introduce something into clinical practice and then see whether it's helpful afterwards, " she said in a telephone interview.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, that is exactly the way the system works. After a drug is approved by the FDA, it may be withdrawn, as many have lately, after it has been found to kill the patients.)

Martin Tramer of Hopitaux Universitaires in Geneva, head of the second research group, had slightly more encouraging results in looking at treatment for chemotherapy-related sickness.

His team, analysing studies involving more than 1,300 patients, found cannabinoids were more effective than some conventional drugs but concluded that potentially serious side effects would limit widespread use.

" The really important point is that where we have good alternatives, we should not use cannabis, which is not as effective and also causes adverse effects, " said Kalso.
(MarijuanaNews note: The best two-word explanation for marijuana prohibition is still " bad journalism. " )
